en: Success! Homage to Tārā.

[1.1] Here, this Master Śāntideva, desiring to compose the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* in order to lead others into the Bodhisattva vow and to establish himself firmly therein, first says "the Sugatas," etc., for the sake of maintaining proper conduct and so forth. In this verse, six topics are set forth: the homage to the Three Jewels and to those worthy of veneration such as preceptors; the subject matter (*abhidheya*); the purpose (*prayojana*) which is the connection between them; the lack of independence; and the absence of redundancy.

In this context, the "restraint of the sons of the Sugata" is the subject matter (*abhidheya*). Its expression through this treatise is the verbal designation (*abhidhāna*). The relationship characterized by the status of the designator and the designated is understood through implication. Furthermore, the ultimate purpose (*prayojana*) of this subject matter is understood to be the perfection of Buddhahood. The remainder is easy to understand. The *dharmakāya* is that which is liberated from all substrates (*upadhi*); or, alternatively, "Dharma" refers to the teaching (*pravacana*) resulting from realization (*adhigama*).

Furthermore, this subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth must necessarily be stated at the outset by those who possess discernment (*prekṣāvat*), as they constitute the necessary conditions for their engagement. Moreover, prostration to the Three Jewels and the like, while generating merit, also wards off the demerit that is its opposite. Thus, for the author, the commentator, and the listeners, there is a benefit (*anuśaṃsa*) regarding the undertaking of the composition, the explanation, and the hearing [respectively]. Although [the stages] such as the *gotrabhūmi* exist in many ways due to their distinctions, [this is stated] in brief. By the phrase "this" (*idam*), the uninterrupted nature of merit is indicated.

"Inferior" refers to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and others. "Adhimukti" means faith or aspiration. [1.21–22] "The removal of a headache by means of a mantra or medicine": the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is used here as before, in the sense of "it is grasped. "How much more so? (*kim uta*) indicates an even greater degree. "Suffering like a headache" (*śūlam iva śūlam*): this refers to immeasurable (*apramita*) suffering in saṃsāra. "Grasping through immeasurable merit" (*aprameyeṇa puṇyena grahaḥ*). [1.23] By the words "of whom," etc., the uniqueness of such a specific state of mind is expressed. "Of whom" (*kasya*) refers generally to a sentient being; "of the mother," etc., specifies that very person.

Of the deities, such as Soma, Varuṇa, and others; or of the sages, such as the Śiṣṭas and others. Or "beings" refers to those who exist, even those far away or yet to come—there has never arisen in anyone other than a Bodhisattva such a longing, whose object is the removal of all suffering and the bestowal of all virtues for those very people, such as one's mother and so forth. "This" refers to the one possessing the qualities just described. "Whence and how? expresses wonder, for such a resolve for the welfare of others does not exist in anyone else besides him.

[1.26] There is also benefit by way of the bodhicitta known as "Joy of the World. [1.27] To the question "How is this so?", he says: The *praṇidhicitta* (the mind of aspiration), which consists merely of wishing for the welfare [of others] while lacking actual practice, is distinguished; that is, it becomes superior [to the mere wish] through the exertion (*udyama*) of the nature of the *prasthānacitta* (the mind of application). [1.28] Since sentient beings themselves are already proficient in attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, one might ask, "What is the use of exertion for the sake of their happiness? To this he says: "Suffering," etc.

With the intention of escaping the sufferings of hunger and so forth, one undergoes even more suffering—such as that of the hells—through acts like taking life. [1.29] With all forms of happiness, both physical and mental. [1.30] For a Bodhisattva dwelling in such a manner, from where could another possess merit equal to his? [1.31] For it is said: "When a service has been rendered, one should return it; one should repay the favor."

What can be said of the noble Bodhisattva who, though unasked and not having been prompted to offer assistance by a return favor, acts for the benefit of others? What can be said of his greatness? It is beyond the range of words, because it transcends verbal expression. "Meager food" refers to that which is not excellent. "With contempt" means that those entering the almshouse are struck with kicks, slaps, and the like. "Merely" implies the exclusion of giving clothing and other such gifts. And by that [meager food], one’s time is spent for half the day at most.

Because one seeks food in the evening after having eaten at midday, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). [1.33] Furthermore, he asks "how much more so? (*kiṃ vā*) to show that a Bodhisattva who possesses such generosity is even more worthy of worship, as this is the opposite of the aforementioned case: for beings who are devoid of limits, his gift perfectly fulfills every desire for an unlimited duration of time. Because there is no limit to the exhaustion of either the sky-like person or the sky itself, it is inexhaustible; for those two are themselves inexhaustible.

For one who bestows gifts such as food and clothing, how could there not be worthiness of honor? The meaning is that there certainly would be. [1.34] Thus, regarding a Bodhisattva who is thus constituted and whose sole essence is the welfare of others, he shows that faith and lack of faith are the causes of happiness and suffering, and must therefore be diligently adopted or avoided respectively. [1.35] In this manner, according to the sequence stated, the fruit of the maturation of merit is greater than the fruit of the maturation of previously committed evil karma.

If it is argued that turbidity and lack of clarity may exist in a bodhisattva, but clarity cannot, the author replies with the word "great" (*mahatā*). This refers to the power and difficulty involved in having well-cultivated body, speech, and mind. "Auspicious" refers to forms such as clarity and so forth. [1.36] Now, because the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) possesses many benefits, the author—who is himself clear-minded—celebrates the bodies of bodhisattvas and the bodhisattvas themselves as the basis for the arising of that [thought], saying "wherein. "That" refers to what was just mentioned.

The particle *api* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). By contriving some pretext, one performs an act of harm; yet, as in the *Maitrībalajātaka*, the *Pañcaka-jātaka*, and others, this results in a connection with the happiness of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and so forth. [1. Colophon: This concludes the section on the benefits of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Memory (*smṛti*).

[2.1] Now, since the vow is to be taken preceded by worship of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he describes that mental worship with the words beginning "taccitta" (that mind). [2.7] But why is worship performed by the mind alone and not directly? He says: "I am meritless. [2.9] "I shall transcend"—this is because there is no regard for sounds, as in the case of the phrase "grasping," etc. [2.10] With the words beginning "ratnojjvala" (blazing with jewels), he again describes mental worship. [2.20] With the words beginning "ataḥ param" (beyond this), worship is described in general terms.

[2.27] He states the confession of sins with the words beginning "I declare for the sake of its purification," based on the principle that restraint ascends instantaneously into a purified continuum. [2.30] He speaks according to their importance with the words beginning "In the Three Jewels. [2.31] With the words beginning "Many," he addresses [the faults] such as haste and distraction. [2.33] With the words beginning "And how," he expresses a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding sin. [2.36–37] Regarding the passage beginning "They will not become unpleasant," he provides the logical justification with the words beginning "That and that."

[2.44] To the question, "What then is this sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*)? he says: "The cutting off of limbs," and so forth. [2.51] And toward that Protector, Avalokita. [2.53] The messengers of Yama, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, and so on. "Vajrin" refers to Vajrapāṇi. [2.55] With the words "transient diseases" and so forth, he censures himself. "Transient" means not long-lasting. There are one hundred untimely deaths (*akālamṛtyu*), and one timely death (*kālamṛtyu*). These are produced by the humors of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and their combination (*saṃnipāta*).
Thus, there are four hundred and four diseases. Even by a single one being provoked, [disease arises]. "In which" refers to those diseases, and "of which" refers to those [specific] diseases.

For formerly, when this very Blessed One was the King of Kāśi named Padma, the humans of Jambudvīpa were afflicted by a great and incurable disease. Having reported their condition to the king, he summoned the physicians and commanded them, "Treat [them]. They replied, "Great King, there is a single medicine, the flesh of the Rohita fish, but that cannot be obtained," and thus they withdrew. This Jātaka is to be applied here.

[2.58] Regarding the reason for the reproach, "one who is exceedingly heedless": in places such as the Avīci hell, which measure a thousand yojanas, and where the lifespan is not exhausted for a long duration such as a great eon (mahākalpa), why indeed do I not remain? [2.59] Therefore, "this very day. [2.61] Of the gurus, the Buddhas and so forth. [2.64] By a fool, that is, by an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). [2.66] "May they accept" means may they know. "Not good" refers to the restraint from non-action. [2. col. In the second [chapter], mindfulness.

[3.1] Because there is a resting or cessation (*viśrama*) from the experience of the suffering of the hells and so forth in those realms when one experiences the happiness that is the fruit of virtuous deeds among gods and others; for this reason, [the word *viśrāma*] follows the instrumentive case (*anukaraṇasya*). Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is used here in the sense of "covering" (*chādye*), which is a form of praise. Because it is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*) of joy (*pramoda*), it likewise includes the body and speech characterized by the utterance of such words and the shedding of tears. Thus, it is called "happiness" (*sukham*).

The meaning is: "May that which was performed by them for whatever purpose be accomplished for them. [3.2] Following the rejoicing in mundane virtue, there is the rejoicing in supramundane goodness, beginning with the words "In saṃsāra... and so forth. Liberation (*nirmokṣa*) refers to the two types of enlightenment or the mind directed toward them. [3.8] The eon (*kalpa*) comes to an end through weapons, disease, and famine, lasting respectively for seven days, seven months, and seven years.

[3.9] Various requisites, such as beds, seats, clothing, food, ornaments, ointments, and so forth; [3.10] I relinquish these to sentient beings, I give them—this merit consisting of the nature of giving and so on—without regard for any return favor or karmic maturation. [3.11] It is the relinquishing of all contaminated things, such as one’s own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). [3.12] Just as pleasure [is felt] from a blow or the like, because it is [experienced] by him in that way; [3.13] may they sport within my aggregates and so forth, remaining full of playfulness through this form, whether even or uneven.

[3.14] Those things which bring them happiness occur exactly as they do; the meaning is that they are blameless. [3.16] They will falsely accuse them with groundless reproach; they will mock and deride them, as will others who are indifferent or even well-disposed. [3.20–21] Likewise, through such retention, there is a lack of immersion [in the teachings], yet by means of removing cold, heat, and so forth—this is what is called the giving of one’s person and so on, beginning with the words "of one's person" (*ātmabhāvādi*).

[3.22] Now, having understood the difficulty of obtaining the endowment of the favorable conditions (*kṣaṇasaṃpad*) and the great benefits of generating the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and having performed worship and the gift of one’s own body and so forth with the verse beginning "That mind" (*taccitta*), one who is perfected in the preliminary application generates the spirit of enlightenment with the verse beginning "Just as it was taken" (*yathā gṛhītam*). The spirit of enlightenment is the desire for perfect awakening for the sake of others. [3.31] "Churning" (*mathana*) is the investigation by means of wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth. [3.32] "Arrived from that and that state" (*tasyās tasyā gater āgatāḥ*) means those who have come from various states of existence.

And this state of being a constant feast of happiness is by way of its suitability; and it is through happiness pertaining to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) that [the beings] are not established in enlightenment until the interval—that is, in the interim. In the third [chapter], there is mindfulness (*smṛti*).

[4.1] Having explained the nourishment of the subsequent [practice], he begins to demonstrate the practice itself with the words "enlightenment belongs to one for whom practice is the essence," and so forth. It is "firm" because it is not abandoned even at the cost of one's life. "Free from sloth" means devoid of indolence (*tandri*). [4.2] Even after having accepted [the vow], it is appropriate to have such a doubt as, "Shall I do it or not? [4.4] Having made the vow, "May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world," [one acts] through action consisting of corresponding activity. "Having deceived" means having misled.

What destination is there other than the miserable states? For it is said: "By means of the mind," and even more so by means of speech. But surely, did not the noble Śāriputra, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva, propitiate ten thousand Buddhas; yet, being harassed by Māra, he abandoned the thought of awakening, attained the awakening of a śrāvaka, and thereby benefited many sentient beings? To the question of how this can be so, he says: "He knows. [This is known] by those who are inconceivable and by those of the present day; [he knows] those respective objects.

And this is because, even if one abandons the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one does not abandon the thought of liberation. [4.8] "By that very same" means by the very fact of being exerted for the sake of sentient beings, as was promised. [4.11] By the force of transgressions, one is dragged backward; and by the power of the thought of awakening, one is led forward. [4.12] "By the palm" means by going downward through a succession of miserable rebirths (*durgati*). [4.13] To the objection, "Surely, through meeting with some Tathāgata, you will attain a happy rebirth (*sugati*) alone," he says: "Immeasurable."

[4.14] Therefore, even now, if one remains thus—slack in the vows of training (*śikṣāsamvara*) due to not turning away from unwholesome states—there is "cutting" of the hands, feet, and so forth by means of a knife or similar weapon; there is "piercing" of those very same limbs by means of a spear or similar weapon. [4.15] Such a collection of conditions is difficult to obtain. Thus, he says "When? to indicate that it is appropriate to apply effort precisely toward this end. "Human existence" refers to being free from the unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*). "Fitness for the practice of the wholesome" results from the non-deficiency of the sense faculties. [4.16] It is "free from affliction" because it is devoid of fear from thieves and the like.

[4.26] Furthermore, he reflects for himself: "In some way or other... The ground of benefit consists of the perfection of the opportune moment (*kṣaṇasaṃpat*) and association with spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). And even though he knows through discernment (*viveka*), those very things to which he was previously led... [4.28] "Devoid of hands and so forth" because they are formless (*amūrtatvāt*). [4.30] "To bring together"—because of the impermanence indicated by the negative particle (*nañ*). [4.31] "Powerful" because they are the causes of immediate succession (*anantarya*) and because they cannot be remedied. [4.34] "Calamities" refers to the sufferings of hell and so forth.

[4.35] Because the appearance of executioners, messengers of Yama, and so forth, is produced from this, they are the "slayers of those to be slain. Within the house of the intellect is the cage consisting of greed. [4.36] "Yoke" (*dhūḥ*) means the burden (*dhūḥ*), namely the vow (*pratijñā*). Here, it refers to the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*). [4.37] Since life ends in death, death is inherent to its very nature. [4.38] Dejection through despondency is a state of mental contraction; it is caused by hundreds of calamities, hundreds of sufferings, or hundreds of fatigues.

[4.39] “Without cause” means precisely by being devoid of the purpose of purifying the next world and so forth. [4.42] Thinking, “I shall become one who does not turn back,” he considers, “In that case, I would be like a madman. [4.43] To the objection—“Since even the attachment to the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) must itself be abandoned because it is itself an affliction, how can there be such a thing as ‘not turning back’?”—he says, “Elsewhere”: those afflictions which are obstacles to perfect enlightenment are to be abandoned; however, those of that other kind are not to be destroyed until the completion of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*). This is the meaning.

[4.44] One might object: "Since it is difficult to uproot due to being long-acquainted, is it not better not to bow down at all toward the afflictions? To this he says, "Let them fall," and so forth. [4.45] By the words "of one who has been exiled," etc., he states that the enemy of the afflictions is easily uprooted. [4. col. In the fourth [chapter], mindfulness.

[5.1] Having taken up the bodhisattva vow, one must train according to one's ability in the practice of what is prescribed and the avoidance of what is prohibited; this is stated by the words beginning with "the training" (*śikṣām*). [5.2–8] By this sequence, it is demonstrated that the mind alone is primary. [5.9] One might object: "Generosity and the other perfections are characterized by the removal of poverty and so forth; how then can the mind be primary even in those cases? To this he says, "not poor" (*adaridram*). [5.10] "All one's possessions" (*sarvasvam*) refers to both external and internal things.

[5.11] But since the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) consists even more fundamentally of the nature of the mind, he says "fishes and so forth. By the word "and so forth," objects such as the property of others, the wives of others, and false speech are included; for elsewhere, by leading them away, they are no longer seen. The phrase "I shall not kill" is an illustration that includes "I shall not steal," and so on. [5.12] When [the fish] are killed, one does not take account of the harm done to them; when they are killed, one does not act out of anger toward their own interests. [5.13] He explains this very point with an illustration beginning with "the earth."

[5.15] By the words "even together with," etc., the nature of the mind as being characterized by diligence (*vīrya*)—which consists of enthusiasm for the wholesome—is made clear. Even when accompanied by body and speech, if its activity toward the wholesome is sluggish, it is not such [diligence]. Rather, it belongs to one who is skillful and adept at the wholesome; it is like the state of being a *Brahmā* or a *Brahmapurohita*, and so forth. [5.16] But meditation (*dhyāna*), characterized by one-pointedness of mind, is the mind itself; thus he says, "recitations" (*japa*). Austerities (*tapas*) refer to the vows of a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and so on.

[5.17] Because it is either distracted by something else or impaired by torpor and so forth, the mind is in vain; for it is either of extremely meager fruit or useless for the intended task. But as for wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no dispute that it is indeed the mind itself. Thus he says: "Suffering" is *saṃsāra*; "bliss" is *nirvāṇa*. "In the sky" means because it dwells in the space of the ether. Those who practice the service of the five fires, the plucking out of hair, and so forth, act fruitlessly.

Because it maintains the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena (*dharma*), it is the "thing" (*vastu*); because all things are entirely complete within their own self-nature, they are of the nature of mind (*cittarūpa*). Since it is not the sphere of experience for the foolish, the mind is "secret"; it has not been cultivated by means of a discerning intellect (*buddhi*), nor has it been repeatedly stabilized. Therefore, the meaning is that this [discerning intellect] is also simply the mind itself, as it consists of the nature of a discerning intellect.

[5.18] Since the mind alone is thus preeminent in all circumstances, it should be well-established through mindfulness and well-guarded through vigilant awareness (*saṃprajanya*). One who possesses such restraint should attend to the mind in this way. [5.20] [The origin of the Saṃghāta hell arises] from the impact of mountain peaks in that form... [text missing here]. [5.21] Wicked people are the provokers of patience, and women are the provokers of the loss of ethical discipline (*śīla*); thus, two things are proclaimed. One is not broken by a transgression through its commission, nor is one made to fall from ethical discipline.

[5.22] Furthermore, he says "gains" (*lābhā*) because the mind is to be thus gladdened. [5.23] A salutation with joined palms is performed; having performed the salutation, a prayer is made. For what purpose? He says, "and mindfulness" (*smṛtim ca*). Since the mind cannot be protected by each [factor] individually, there are two *ca*s (and-s) to indicate their mutual dependence. In that context, "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the recollection of what has been enjoined and what has been prohibited, as appropriate.

[5.24] Moving within the states of body and mind, the discernment (*saṃprajanya*) that consists in such reflections as "I am moving" while guarding, or "I shall guard," and so forth, [applies] to all actions such as walking, eating, and the like. [5.26] Likewise, "disturbed by these two" means impaired; "in all actions" refers to reciting, studying, and so forth. [5.27] "Many" refers to the further fault in the absence of discernment (*asaṃprajanya*). [5.28] "Absence of discernment" is another [fault], for it is a thief because it steals the wealth of virtue; it follows the path of robbing the watchman of mindfulness (*smṛti*).

"Robbed" means those whose wealth of virtue has been plundered. He clarifies this very point with the words "by the afflictions" (*kleśa*). Like a *piśāca* or similar being, he seeks an opening; having found an entry point in the form of lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), he acts. With reference to mindfulness (*smṛti*), he says "therefore": because in the absence of mindfulness there is an absence of clear comprehension, and thus these many faults arise; therefore, the mind itself is the gateway for the afflictions, since they enter the house of the mental continuum through it alone. And that mindfulness arises from intense reverence.

Having understood the greatness of *śamatha*, he says "by the preceptor" (*upādhyāya*), because mindfulness may arise for some even through other means. Instruction (*anuśāsanī*) is the teaching for the sake of protecting what has been attained; this also includes *avavāda* (guidance) by implication. Likewise, there is the inclusion of fellow celibates (*brahmacārin*) who are to be honored, whether they be teachers or others. For those of merit who apply themselves to recitation, study, and so forth, [mindfulness] is easy to achieve and without hardship. [5.32] Shame (*trapā*) is a sense of modesty regarding unwholesome states; it is reverence for the training and fear of transgressing it.

"So be it" (*tathā*) refers to the conjunction of the causes for mindfulness. "The recollection of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as well" indicates another benefit. He says "clear comprehension" (*saṃprajanya*) because mindfulness alone is the cause for both the arising and the persistence of clear comprehension. "In order to protect the wealth of the wholesome from the thieves that are the afflictions" [5.34]. He says "previously" in order to prohibit fruitless movement; [the mind] is like a piece of wood because it is devoid of the activity of the eyes and other faculties. He clarifies this very point by saying "fruitless" [5.35].

[5.36] For a human being approaching, there is merely a reflection; it is a mere shadow intended as a greeting because Bodhisattvas are the first to speak. [5.37] Fear refers to thieves, tigers, and so forth. "In the four directions" means sequentially. This is a collective compound (*samāhāra*). One should look back with the entire body by turning the whole direction behind one, but not by twisting the neck backward, as that is improper conduct (*anācāra*). [5.38] One should move forward; one should retreat backward. This is for the sake of avoiding the taking of life, falling into precipices, and other such dangers.

In all postures, such as lying down and so forth, one should practice after having understood the purpose, which is the welfare of oneself and others. [5.39] By saying "with the body thus," he teaches *saṃprajanya* (clear comprehension). "Thus" refers to sitting and so forth. Having initiated and stabilized the action of sitting and so forth, at a later time, one asks "how?"—that is, by means of that same posture or another? If it is another, the body should be established as before. [5.40]

He speaks of the examination of the mind with the word "having analyzed" (*nirūpya*). Dharma is that which benefits oneself and others. Even when bound, it is to be analyzed. [5.41] Where? Having withdrawn it from what has entered into another object, it should be applied to the subject at hand; it should be regarded with equanimity as it flows by its own nature. [5.42] In cases of danger from fire and so forth, or during festivals for the Buddhas and so forth; in cases such as frivolous chatter through compliance with others; or when one is unable [to act], acting according to one's own pleasure while perceiving the welfare of sentient beings—there is no offense even if one does not remain in meditative concentration.

Why? Regarding the word "giving" (*dāna*): even if one has reached excellence in ethical discipline (*śīla*) through giving, for one who is training in the lower training, there is no offense in neglecting it immediately thereafter if one is unstable in the higher training. This is because one considers, "This is the time for giving, not for ethical discipline. [5.43] Even when shifting toward the side of the wholesome, if there is a possibility of obstructing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), that [practice] should not be undertaken. Thus he says "that which": having understood through both reasoning and scripture, that which is meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth. [5.44] Both were previously and subsequently commenced.

[5.45] He says "not manifold" (*nāna*) to indicate that nothing fruitless should be done. [5.47] That which is to be practiced has been stated in the context of the state of non-affliction (*asaṃkleśa*), having been examined. [5.49] "Utprāsa" is physical harassment. [5.50] "Saṃrambha" is attachment to quarrels and the like. [5.54] A "hero" is a bodhisattva; by means of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), such as the meditation on the foul (*aśubhādi*), one overcomes passion and so forth. [5.55] "Respect" (*ādara*) is attentiveness. "Veneration" (*gaurava*) is humility toward those worthy of honor. One who is "afraid of failing" is cautious regarding any lapse.

[5.56] Since that which is pleasant to one is unpleasant to another, they possess conflicting desires; therefore, he is without remorse. Because of this affliction, their conduct is mutually contradictory; thus, he feels compassion for them. [5.57] [He brings them] under his own power and the power of sentient beings. [5.59] Furthermore, in order to fix the mind, he speaks of the examination of the body with the words "by vultures," etc. Otherwise, one would be devoid of mind. Therefore, because the mind is primary, the vow of the mind alone is superior, not the vow of the body.

[5.60] To the objection that such dependence is illogical for something useless, he says: "She protects. [5.61] If it is argued that this is because she was previously accepted, he says: "You do not accept her. [5.66] He says: "It is logical," meaning that this is appropriate because there is no other purpose. [5.67] He says: "In this way," meaning that even so, one should not harbor dogmatic attachment. [5.75] He speaks of the destruction of envy regarding "well-spoken words. [5.76] He says "and behind one's back" in order to eliminate flattery.

But when another is speaking, even in their presence, one should follow along with them [5.77]. The removal of intolerance toward the virtues of others is expressed by the words "all," and so forth. By means of the virtues belonging to others—such as being a grammarian—which are produced through the efforts of others [5.79], one is free from the suspicion of fault and thus confident. It is motivated by compassion, not born of passion or other such emotions. It is soft and not harsh; it is in a low tone and not loud, because it is articulated in such a way that the listener may achieve understanding.

By this, the entire process of following [the practice] has been explained, because awakening (bodhi) is rooted therein. Speaking ill of those who possess patience regarding the profound Dharma; punishing ascetics; giving and taking away the Three Jewels; abandoning one who is practicing tranquility (*śamatha*); offering to those engaged in study what is not conducive to concentration; renouncing the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); out of stinginess, not giving wealth or the Dharma to those who are suffering and without protectors; striking another out of anger; refusing to accept the requests of others; rejecting the Mahāyāna; and proclaiming a counterfeit of the true Dharma.

These three, along with the one concerning women, constitute the *pārājika* offenses because they cause the destruction of the vow (*saṃvara*). Laziness (*ālasya*) is the unserviceability of body and mind.

"Self-submissiveness" (*ātmavidheyatā*) is being under one's own control. These form a copulative compound (*dvandva*). This [collection] is joined with those not previously mentioned. Equanimity toward self and others and the exchange of self and others will be explained in the section on meditation (*dhyāna*).

This entire section is also a summary for the purpose of abandoning laziness. [7.17] In that regard, he first explains the absence of despondency: "There is no despondency whatsoever. This means: from such a form of mental attention as follows. [7.18] "This" refers to what will be stated beginning with "those also," and so forth. "Those also" refers to Śākyamuni and the others in former times. [7.19] How much more so, then, in the case of one who possesses excellence? And therefore, because there is no abandonment of the system of the Omniscient One, which teaches what is to be discarded and what is to be adopted—how could it be that [despondency] does not exist at all? It is certainly not the case that it does not exist.

[7.20] For this reason as well, one should fix the mind precisely upon this: that what is heavy regarding the suffering of *saṃsāra* is light for the sake of awakening, and what is light regarding the suffering of hardships is heavy due to delusion—that is, a state of perversion arising from a lack of investigation. [7.21] He says this very thing with the words "must be cut": it must be cut by the severing of hands, feet, and so forth, according to the power of various karmas; it must be pierced by spears, lances, and the like; it must be burned by the fires of hell and so forth; and it must be split by flaming saws and the like.

And enlightenment does not arise through this suffering, because its accumulations have not been acquired. Where is this? It refers to that which arises from difficult practices; it is limited because it lasts for only a short time, like the pain caused by extracting a life-long, deeply embedded thorn. For this reason as well, he says "all" to show that what must be undertaken is difficult: by means of the sufferings produced by actions such as jumping or cooking, many births and so forth are endured, while the form of the practice for enlightenment is but slight.

[7.24] Furthermore, the Blessed One, the supreme physician, did not bestow nor prescribe this practice—consisting of such acts as decapitation—even though it was appropriate, for beginners. This is because, by means of a gentle approach, he addressed those who are greatly afflicted and seized by the long-standing diseases of passion and so forth. [7.25] He prescribed a treatment that is indeed sweet "at the outset. Even when giving merely vegetables, roasted flour, balls of food, and the like, which can be easily abandoned [by others].

"One acts accordingly" means that by means of a specific method, one proceeds in such a sequence that through the practice of giving, one may eventually relinquish even one's own flesh. To the question, "How could one perform this difficult task? he says, "When... (verse 7.27): "When, through the excellence of the practice of giving or through the practice of selflessness... Now, one might ask: "How can worldly suffering, which lasts for so long, be endured? To this he says, "Not suffering": one is not suffering because of having abandoned the three types of evil.

Because of his wisdom, he is one who has ascertained the selflessness of both [person and phenomena]. [7.28] False conceptualization consists of the conceptualization of a self and what belongs to a self. Having demonstrated that there is an absence of suffering due to the absence of its cause, and that there is indeed happiness because of the presence of its cause, he says, "by merit. Thus, endowed with both kinds of happiness and possessing compassion, by what suffering could he be afflicted? By none whatsoever. Or rather, for what reason is there no suffering? Because of the absence of the cause of suffering, there is none whatsoever.

[7.29] One might object: "Surely, because it is not delayed, the awakening of a śrāvaka alone should be adopted by those who possess discernment. To this he says, "Exhausting... [7.30] With the word "thus," he concludes the section on non-despair. [7.31] With the passage beginning "the power of zeal" (*chandasthāma*), there is an enumeration of the array of powers (*balavyūha*). Among these, *chanda* is the desire for the wholesome, distinct from mere enthusiasm (*utsāha*). *Sthāma* is firmness once an undertaking has been begun. *Rati* is attachment to virtuous deeds. *Mukti* is the temporary relinquishing of an undertaking when one is unable to carry it out.

This fourfold army is for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, because this vigor is the cause thereof, and because vigor brings about all forms of excellence. In that regard, since aspiration (*chanda*) is of great utility, he first states the cause for its arising with the words "aspiration. Aspiration is the longing for the wholesome, born from the fear of the sufferings of hell and so forth produced by the unwholesome; and the benefits (*anuśaṃsā*) pertain only to the wholesome. [7.32] Now he describes the operation of power (*bala*) with the word "thus" (*evam*), according to the method of the previously stated continuity; the adverse side (*vipakṣa*) consists of laziness and so forth.

By uprooting [the afflictions] through the practice of correct application (*pratipatti*). Pride (*māna*) is indeed stability. Regarding the mastery of intent (*tātparya*), it is mentioned immediately after the array of forces (*balavyūha*). By means of their capacities: [7.33] therein, he speaks of the generation of aspiration (*chandotpādana*): "Immeasurable" because each one, such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, has infinite subdivisions. [7.34] Even a mere atom of the destruction of faults. [7.36] "Marvelous" because of its rarity. [7.37] "For this reason also, nothing fruitless has been attained. "Services" (*kārāḥ*) are acts of benefit (*upakārāḥ*), starting from the writing of the true Dharma (*saddharma*) and so forth.

[7.38] They are afflicted by physical and mental sufferings; they experience the state of being pierced by a thorn within the womb and the belly. [7.39] From where, then, could such a calamity arise? It is said: "O you who have zeal for the Dharma! Calamity is characterized by the absence of even a trace of the destruction of faults. Thus he expresses a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). [7.51] Having stated the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "Even when I am engaged in lowly tasks" refers to carrying burdens and the like. Even when I have become a servant to sentient beings, pride—which causes the ruin of great purposes—is not the engagement in lowly work itself.

[7.52] Regarding the secondary affliction of pride (*māna*), he says "dead. If, among the secondary afflictions, the mind should become weak because pride has been suppressed, then even a minor occurrence arising from a slight secondary affliction constitutes a calamity (*āpad*). Why is it called "dead"? [7.53] He asks, "From where, then, does the possibility of calamities arise? and answers with "despair" (*viṣāda*). For one who is devoid of mental exaltation, calamities are easily encountered due to despondency and the resulting lack of effort. Such a person is "upset" (*vyutthita*) by the secondary afflictions and has fallen into error.

By means of mindfulness and clear comprehension, one who exerts effort so that these [faults] find no opportunity remains invincible even to the great afflictions. [7.54] With the words "Therefore," he concludes the section on the power of steadfastness (*sthāmabala*). "Firm" means unshakable by pride; otherwise, as for the phrase "the three worlds," [he asks]: what kind of desire for victory is this? He says: "Lions" because they cannot be assailed by any of the beasts that are the Māras. [7.56] If that is so, then those possessed of pride are also praiseworthy for the sake of conquering enemies; to this he replies with the word "those who. [7.55]

[They are] conquered by pride and overwhelmed by pride. [7.57] To the question "Whence comes the proud one? and further, "What is the fault in pride?", he says: "By means of pride. Even if they somehow attain human status, they are joyless. [7.58] "Everywhere" means in all places and from all people, they suffer humiliation and defeat. They are wretched and miserable. [7.59] To the question "Who, then, are the proud ones?", he says: "Those. Even though they are surging forth and even though they are powerful, among people including the gods and others, the fruit of victory is Buddhahood.

He demonstrates that such is the state in the condition of Buddhahood. "Victors" (*vijayinaḥ*) means those who have attained victory; "heroes" (*śūrāḥ*) means those possessed of splendor. [7.60] Having established pride (*māna*) with respect to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), he speaks regarding power (*śakti*): "Situated in the midst of the category of defilements" because of being subject to cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*); "arrogant" (*dṛpta*) and "most haughty" (*darpiṣṭha*) due to the possession of power. How so? "Difficult to conquer" (*duryodhana*) because of being hard to defeat. [7.61] He states this very point with an illustration: "Even among the great," and so forth. [7.62] He speaks of the power of delight (*ratibala*) with the words "that which... (*yat*).

"Action" (*karman*) refers to the accumulation of requisites such as meditation, study, and so forth. "In times of distress" means when one encounters adversity. "Addicted to that action" means being intensely attached to it. "Intoxicated by that action" means being greedily devoted to its performance, like one who desires the pleasure that results from games such as gambling. [7.63] Thus, he says "for the sake of happiness" to indicate that even in action there should be delight; for it is not possible that an undertaking could be entirely fruitless, and yet the world does not desist from action.

And for what purpose is the form of meditation and study? [7.64] He says "by desires" (referring to *kāmaiḥ*)—meaning by forms and so forth—in order to show that even while reflecting on this, one should take delight in meritorious action. Just as there is the pain of cutting the tongue when consuming honey stuck on the edge of a razor, so too is there the suffering of birth and so forth from desires even when they are experienced; thus, they are "like that. They are "sweet" because their ripening or transformation results in fruits such as heaven. They are "auspicious" (*śivaiḥ*) because they lead to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) and are the cause of freedom from old age and death.

For this very reason, it was said, "with the nectar of merit" [7.65]. Therefore, under the guise of a conclusion, he reinforces the very delight in action with the words "therefore" (tasmāt). "The end" (*avasāna*) refers to the time of dismissal. The compound *prāptasarāḥ karī* is a *karmadhāraya* containing within it a *bahuvrīhi*. [7.66] He speaks of the power of liberation as "powerful. This refers to the capacity to complete an undertaking once begun; however, if there is no persistence—that is, no following through in a continuous series—then there is destruction in a mere moment.

One may postpone for a time with the intention, "I shall do it later"; and even that which is already well-accomplished should be abandoned out of regard for another superior task, because once that is completed, further effort is of no use. This is an exception to what was previously stated regarding the investigation of the collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*) and so forth. [7.67] Having described the array of forces in its entirety, although *aviṣāda* (absence of despondency) was mentioned first, it is now discussed again within the group beginning with *chanda* (zeal) as something that must necessarily be practiced; he states its essential meaning with the words "afflictions" (*kleśa*).

"Guarding" means restraining. "Firmly" means by not allowing any further opportunity. [7.68] Furthermore, he teaches the intent (*tātparya*) regarding that point: "the sword" refers to battle; "fallen" refers to the loss of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃpramoṣa*); and "when there is a lapse" means while being mindful. [7.69] One might ask: "Should even a subtle fault not be overlooked? To this he says: "poison. It "spreads" means it extends. A "vulnerability" (*chidra*) is of the nature of the loss of mindfulness. Even a minute fault [is like poison]. [7.70] With the words "in oil," he states the intent once more in another way.

Likewise, the practitioner who possesses the bodhisattva vow should be intent on ensuring that no opportunity for a lapse occurs, out of fear of the suffering caused by such a slip. Having said "therefore," he concludes: "One should remedy" means one should perform a remedy through such means as washing the face, the perception of light, and the cultivation of impermanence. Regarding what must be done even when another person has slipped, he says: "In each and every [lapse]" refers to a lapse occurring from the occasional loss of mindfulness; this is what constitutes a lapse.

By this reason—namely, the intention to prevent any opportunity for transgression—even though association and dwelling in one place with learned masters, preceptors, and others have been forbidden, the meaning is that one should remain dependent upon them. Or, "action" refers to the form of admonition and instruction, or it has resulted in the nature of disciplinary action (*daṇḍakarma*) in the event of a transgression. "How indeed" (*kathaṃ nāma*) is an expression used in the sense of hope according to worldly usage. "In these states of entry into the afflictions" (*kleśāvatāradaśāsu*). And it has been said: "By the instruction of the preceptor," and so forth.

[7.74] He speaks of the self being under one's own control with the words "one should make it light. "Light" means acting swiftly. The "self" consists of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Likewise, through the practice of enthusiasm (*utsāha*), there is heedfulness (*apramāda*), which is the application of attention to wholesome qualities. This includes such [teachings] as "heedfulness regarding talk about that is the state of immortality. Even before beginning an action, one should be ready and have gathered all necessary provisions, like a well-tamed horse. [7.75] He clarifies the very point already stated by means of an illustration with the words "just as. The coming and going of the wind is dependent [upon its own power].

In this way, one should apply oneself with enthusiasm. In this way, for one devoted to practice, supernatural powers such as traveling through space and so forth are accomplished. [7. Colophon] Seventh: Mindfulness.

[8.1–2] Because one whose mind is distracted stands, as it were, amidst the fangs of the afflictions which are like *rākṣasa* demons, he begins the section on the body (*kāya*) in order to eliminate distraction, which is the adversary of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Vitarkas" refers to those whose range is the countryside and so forth; since this is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), it includes sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the rest as well. [8.3] In that regard, he first states the reason for not abandoning the world: "Out of affection" (*snehāt*). Affection is attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*); and [it arises] through thirst (*tarṣa*) for gain, honor, fame, and so forth.

This is for the sake of obtaining this affection, for the thirst of the world, and for the reason of not abandoning it. [8.4] Because it is said that one who is well-endowed with calm abiding (*śamatha*) as the cause and insight (*vipaśyanā*), being concentrated in mind, understands things as they truly are; thus, through non-regard and non-attachment toward the entire world—meaning, through lack of delight and lack of attachment—[one acts]. [8.5] He asks "of what" regarding that very lack of delight: "of children, wife, and so forth," which are impermanent. By what cause? "By which. And that which pleases is "dear" (*priya*).

[8.6] He says "not seeing" because even the reality of this [pleasure] does not exist. *Rati* is steadfastness (*dhṛti*). "As before" means as at the time of seeing. [8.7] He states another fault: one neither sees nor knows the faults and virtues that are non-perverted. Through that very delusion (*moha*), one falls away from spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) due to the longing for union with the beloved. By that very delusion, one is consumed by the grief that arises even at a moment's separation.

[8.8] With such thoughts as, "How might this beloved one and our union with him be uninterrupted," and so forth—*dharma* here refers to merit (*puṇya*), because it is included within the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*). [8.9] He establishes this very point regarding the destruction of eternal *dharma* by means of the verse beginning with "by the foolish" (*bālaiḥ*). "By the foolish" means by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Because of their karma-obstructions similar to that [destruction], a miserable rebirth (*durgati*) is certain. That [destruction] is neither desired nor hated by the foolish alone; rather, it is hated by them. Thus, since it causes harm in both worlds, what benefit or happiness could be obtained from its cause? Or rather, what [benefit] has been attained?

Not at all anything. [8.10–11] Having perceived or not perceived their own purpose from moment to moment, respectively; even in a situation of satisfaction, regarding the performance of benefit, happiness, and so forth—why then "what is harmful"? This refers to those fools (*bāla*). "Speech" (*vaca*) follows from the context. [8.12] And one should bring this characteristic of a fool to mind for the sake of distinguishing it: "dualism" (*dvandva*) is dispute (*vivāda*); "intoxication" (*mada*)... [text ends].
